Shri Krishna Chund replied, "Father! you are wise, why do you exalt your sons? Think a little in your mind that the acts of Bhagavat are infinite; no one has to this day ascertained the limits of them. Behold! he shines in every mortal frame, and therefore the world calls him 'The being without passions or human qualities.' He creates, he destroys, he remains mixed with the world, but can never be bound by it. Earth, sky, air, water and fire, the five elements of the body, in them all the power of the lord abides. The sacred precepts of the Vedas have declared this."

O great king! on hearing these words from the mouth of Shri Krishna Chund Jee, Vasudeva, being under the influence of fascination, was silent and remained gazing on the countenance of Hari; then Krishna went thence to his mother, and on seeing her son, Devaki Jee said, "O! Shri Krishna Chund, the root of joy! one grief at times pierces me." Krishna enquired, "What it was?" Devaki Jee replied, "Son! grief for the loss of your six elder brothers, whom Kamsa destroyed, never departs from my mind."

SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! on his saying this, Shri Krishna Chund Jee went to the regions below, having first said to his mother, "Mourn not now, I will bring my brothers here immediately," When Raja Buli received intelligence of Krishna's arrival, he came out to meet him; and, having with great pomp and preparation, spread silken cloths for him to walk upon, escorted him to his own abode; having afterwards seated him on a throne, and put sandal, unbroken rice and flowers upon his forehead, and placed before him perfumes, lamps and consecrated food, Raja Buli worshipped Shri Krishna Chund, then standing before him with joined hands, and glorifying him greatly, he said, "O great king! why have you come here?" Hari replied "Raja! in the age of truth (or in the good age) there was a sage named Mureech, a great, religious student, wise, a speaker of the truth and a devout worshipper of Hari; his wife’s name was Oorna, who had six sons. One day, the six brothers in their youthful state having gone before the Raja (the lord of subjects) laughed; observing that they laughed, the Raja was very angry, and pronounced this curse, 'Go, and descend upon the earth as demons.' O great king! on hearing this curse, the sage’s sons were greatly alarmed, and went and fell at the feet of the Raja; and having beseeched him greatly said, with the utmost humility, 'O sea of compassion! you have pronounced a curse; but be pleased to favour us by saying; when we shall be liberated from it.' Having heard their humble speech, the Raja taking compassion upon them, said, 'When you see Shri Krishna' Chund, you will be released.' O great king! on his saying this, they gave up the ghost, and became the sons of Hurinakoos; then they were born as the sons of Vasudeva, whom Kamsa came and murdered, on their being slain, the delusive power brought them here, and, conferring happiness, placed them in this abode; their mother Devaki mourns for them; for this reason, I am come here, that I may take away my brothers with me and present them to my mother, and remove the anxiety of her mind."

SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said, Raja! when Hari had thus spoken, Raja Buli brought and gave him the six children, and placed before him many presents; then Krishna came thence with his brothers to his mother; who, on seeing her sons, was highly delighted; when the inhabitants heard this, there was joy throughout the city, and the curse pronounced upon the sons terminated.

86.e: SHRI SHUKADEVA JEE said,—Raja! I will now relate how Arjuna carried off Shri Krishna Chund Jee’s sister, Soobhudra, from Dwarka; and how Shri Krishna Chund went and abode in Mithila, listen with attention: when Devaki’s daughter, whose name was Soobhudra, and who was younger than Shri Krishna Jee, was marriageable; Vasudeva Jee having invited several of the descendants of Yadu, and Shri Krishna and Balarama said, "The girl is now of a fit age to be married, to whom shall we give her?" Balarama Ji replied, "It is said, 'That we ought to contract marriage, enmity and friendship with equals; one thing occurs to me, that we ought to marry this girl to Duryodhana, and obtain renown and greatness in the world." Shri Krishna Chund said, "In my opinion, we shall obtain a high reputation in the world by giving her to Arjuna."

SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! on Balarama’s speaking, no one uttered a word; but when Shri Krishna Chund Jee had spoken, all exclaimed, "It is most advisable to marry the girl to Arjuna." Balarama Ji was offended at hearing this, and rose up and went away; and the party present, observing that he was offended, remained silent; when Arjuna afterwards received information of these circumstances, he assumed the disguise of a religious mendicant; and, taking a staff and wooden pot went to Dwarka; and, having selected a convenient spot spread a deer’s skin, and sat upon it: he remained thus for four months during the whole rains, and no one discovered his secret purpose; looking upon him as a guest, they all paid him attention; and, for the sake of Vishnu, entertained affection for him; Krishna knew all his secrets, but did not reveal them to any one.

O great king! one day Baladeva Jee also invited and brought with him Arjuna to an entertainment at ibis house, when Arjuna sat down to eat, he beheld Soobhudra, with a body like the moon, and eyes like the deer. On seeing her Arjuna was fascinated; and, avoiding the gaze of all, began to look upon her with averted glance; and thought to himself, "When will Brahma accomplish what is destined in my fate?" Whilst on the other hand Soobhudra Jee, pleased with the brilliancy of his countenance, was saying to herself, "He is some prince and not a religious mendicant, why is he sad?"

Having thus spoken, Soobhudra Jee went into the house and began to think of obtaining a husband.; and on the other hand, Arjuna, after he had finished eating, came to his seat, and was occupied with all kinds of anxieties as to how he should gain possession of his beloved. Some days afterwards, on the occasion of the festival of Shivùrat, all the inhabitants of the city, male and female, went outside the city to worship Shivù. Soobhudra went there also with her female companions and attendants. Having heard of her going, Arjuna mounted his chariot, and taking his bow and arrows, went there and was ready.

Whilst, O great king! Soobhudra was returning with her female friends after having worshipped Shivù, Arjuna at sight of her abandoned all reserve and modesty; and seizing her by the hand, lifted her into his chariot, and went off. Balarama was greatly enraged, when he heard of it; he took his plough and wooden pestle on his shoulder; his eyes were bloodshot, he spoke in a voice of thunder; "I will now go and utterly destroy him, and will lift up the world and place it upon my forehead, how shall a beggar carry off my beloved sister, Soobhudra? Wheresoever I may catch this religious mendicant, I will destroy him, and search out and utterly destroy all his family."

O great king! Balarama Ji continued to make many idle and very angry speeches, when, having heard what had occurred, Purdiyomun, Unroodrù, Sumboo and other noble descendants of Yadu came into the presence of Baladeva Jee, and said with joined hands, "O great king! if you give us the order, we will lay hold of, and bring your enemy here."

Having proceeded thus far in the narrative, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! when Balarama taking all the descendants of Yadu with him, was ready to go in pursuit of Arjuna, Shri Krishna Chund went and explained to Baladeva all the secrets connected with the carrying off Soobhudra; and said in a tone of the greatest submissiveness, "Brother! Arjuna, in the first place, is the son of our paternal aunt; and in the second, he is my greatest friend; he has committed this act heedlessly, and without due thought; but it is not at all right for us to fight with him; this would be contrary to religion, and contrary to the custom of the world; and whoever might hear of our fighting would say, 'That the friendship of the descendants of Yadu is like a wall of sand.'" On hearing these words, Balarama Ji beating his head, and being greatly enraged said, "Brother! this is a common custom with you to raise a fire, and then run for water; otherwise, if you had not taken part in the business, what power had Arjuna to carry off my sister?" Having thus spoken, Balarama Ji suffered great regret, and was very angry, and looking at his brother dashed his plough and wooden pestle on the ground, and sat down; and all the descendants of Yadu sat down also with him.

SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—Raja! whilst Shri Krishna Chund entered into explanations with them all, Arjuna went home and married Soobhudra, in the manner prescribed by the Vedas. On receiving intelligence of the marriage, Shri Krishna and Balarama Ji sent off to Hastinapura, in charge of a brahmin, clothes, jewels, male and female servants, elephants, horses, chariots and a large sum of money; afterwards Shri Murari, the friend of his worshippers, mounted his chariot and went to Mithila, where there were two worshippers of his, named Sootdeo and Buhoolas, the one a Raja, and the other a brahmin.

O great king! on Krishna's departure, Narada, Vamadeva, Vyasa, Atri, Purshooram, and many other sages came and accompanied Shri Krishna Chund Joe; whatever countries Krishna passed through, the Rajas of them came out to meet him, and worshipped him, and gave him presents; at length, after a journey of some days, Krishna arrived there; when they heard of Hari’s arrival, the two worshippers rose up, and came running hastily to him with presents. During their interview with Krishna, they both placed their presents before him; and, making obeisance, and standing in his presence with joined hands, said, with the utmost submissiveness, "O sea of compassion and brother of the poor! you have shown great mercy, in having allowed sinners like us to see you, and thereby made us pure, and put an end to our being born and dying."

Having recited thus much of the history, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! Shri Krishna Chund, acquainted with the secrets of the heart, having beheld the sincere faith of those two worshippers, assumed two bodily forms, and went and dwelt in the houses of both; they entertained and amused him in an agreeable manner; and Hari made a stay of some days, and made them exceedingly happy; after this, when Krishna having gratified all their wishes, and increased their knowledge, went to Dwarka; the sages and saints took leave of him on the road, and Hari went and abode happily at Dwarka.

87.e: HAVING heard so much of the narrative, Raja Parikshit said to SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee, "O great king! you said, on a former occasion, that the Vedas glorified the supreme deity; explain to me, in order that the doubts of my mind may be removed, how the Vedas offered praise to the Brahma without passions or human qualities?" SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee replied,—O great king! the lord, who is the author of the intellect, of the organs of action and perception, of the mind, soul, religious and moral merit, wealth, desire and salvation, constantly remains in a passionless form, without human qualities, but when he creates the world, he is possessed of all qualities, and assumes his own natural form; for this reason, that one deity is both without, and with passions and qualities.

Having thus said, SHUKADEVA, the sage, added, Raja! Narada Ji on one occasion asked Naranarayana the question you have now asked me. Raja Parikshit said, "O great king! please explain this subject to me, that the perplexities of my mind may be removed."

SHUKADEVA Jee replied, Raja! once on a time during the age of truth, Narada Ji went into the world of truth (that is, the world of the virtuous age) to the place where Naranarayana was sitting engaged with many other sages in devout religious austerities, and enquired, "O great king? be pleased to do me the favour to say, how the Vedas glorify the incorporeal Brahma." Naranarayana said, "Hear me Narada! the perplexity, which you have asked me to explain, is the same as occurred in the world of mortals, at a place where Sunatun and other sages were seated, occupied with religious penance. Sanandana, a sage, then narrated a story, and entirely removed the doubts of all present." Narada Ji said, "O great king! I also dwell there, and if this story had been told, I should have heard it." Naranarayana said, "Narada Ji! this story was told, when you had gone to the white island to visit Bhagavat and, therefore, you did not hear it." Having heard this, Narada Ji said, "O great king! kindly inform me what story was related there," Naranarayana replied, "Listen! Narada, when the sages asked this question, Sanandana, the saint, began to say to them, 'Listen to me! at the time of the general destruction, when fourteen worlds became the semblence of water, then the complete Brahma remained alone asleep, when Bhagavan wished to create the world, the Vedas having come forth from his breath and joined their hands, sang praises to him, just as bards, by singing songs of eulogy of his renown very early in the morning, might awaken a Raja, who was asleep in his own house; in order, that being awake, he might quickly perform any business he had to do.'"

Having proceeded thus far in the story, Naranarayana added, "Listen to me, O Narada! the Vedas having come forth from the mouth of the lord were saying, 'O lord! awake quickly and create the world, and remove your deceptive power far from the minds of animated beings; then they will recognize your appearance; your deceptive power is predominant, and deprives all beings of intelligence; the being who escapes from it, will have knowledge to understand you. O lord! no one except you can reduce this power to subjection; he, in whose breast you dwell in the form of knowledge, overcomes this deceptive power; otherwise, who has ability to escape from the influence of this power? You are the creator of all; all animated beings, having derived their origin from you, are contained in you; just as many things being produced from the earth, are again mixed up in the earth; whoever worships or glorifies any god whatsoever, worships and glorifies you, just as a man may make many ornaments of gold, and give them various names, but it is still gold; so you have many forms; and consider this point, that not one of those forms is any thing, and that on what sidesoever we look, there you are presented to our sight. O lord! your deceptive power is infinite; this power becoming the three qualities of truth, passion and darkness; having assumed three forms, and created the universe, preserves and destroys it; no one has discovered its mystery, and no one ever will discover it; wherefore, it is right for an animated being to abandon all desires and meditate upon you; his welfare depends upon his doing so.'"

O great king! having proceeded thus far in his story, Naranarayana said to Narada, "Narada! when Sanandana, the sage, having related this history of a former age, had removed the perplexities of all their minds, then Sunuk and the other sages offered worship to Sanandana according to the sacred precepts of the Vedas."

Having related thus much of the history, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—Raja! whoever shall hear this conversation of Narayana and Narada, shall without doubt obtain the fulfilment of all his desires, and be saved hereafter. The account of the complete Brahma, which the Vedas sang of, Sanandana, the sage, recited to Sunuk and other saints, then Naranarayana related it before Narada; and Vyasa obtained it from Narada; and Vyasa explained it to me, and I have now mentioned it to you; whoever shall hear or relate this history, shall obtain whatever benefits he desires, whatever virtue there is in penance, sacrifice, gifts, fasting and pilgrimage, there is the same merit in reciting and hearing this history.

88.e: SHRI SHUKADEVA JEE said,—O great king! the works of Bhagavat are wonderful; every one knows this, whoever worships Hari will be poor; and by serving other gods, a man will be rich. Compare the state and habits of Hari and Mahadeva; one is the husband of Luchmee, the other of Devee; the one wears a garland of flowers, the other, a necklace of skulls; the former has a quoit in his hand, the latter a trident; one supports the earth; the other, the Ganges; one plays upon a pipe, the other, upon a cow’s horn; one is lord of the celestial paradise, the other, an inhabitant of Kailasa, the former besmears his body with sandal, the latter rubs ashes on it; one wears cloth, the other, a tiger’s skin; one reads the Vedas, the other, the science of Astrology; one rides upon the sovereign of the feathered race, the other, upon the bull Nandi; one dwells among cowherds' children, the other, amongst ghosts and goblins. The habits and nature of each of the two lords are the reverse of those of the other. Fix your affections on either of the two according to the nature of your desires."

Having recited thus much of the history, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! Shri Krishna said to the Raja Yudhishthira,—"O Yudhishthira! I destroy by degrees all the wealth of him, to whom I show favour: because brothers, wives, sons and relations abandon the poor, and then a spirit of devotion springs up in their minds; and, from being occupied in religious devotion, they, having abandoned the fascinations of riches and the world, become free from all attachments, and worship me with zealous attention, and through the glory of their adoration, obtain an everlasting emancipation from matter, and a reunion with the deity." After having thus spoken, SHUKADEVA Jee added,—O great king! by worshipping other gods, the desires of the mind are fulfilled, but final salvation is not obtained.

After having related this story, the sage said to Raja Parikshit,—"O great king! on one occasion as Bikasoor, the son of Kashyapa, came out of his house, desiring to perform penance, he met Narada, the sage, on the road. On seeing Narada Ji he made a salutation; and, standing before him with joined hands, enquired, with the utmost humility, "O great king! which of the three deities Brahma, Vishnu or Mahadeva grants boons most quickly, do me the kindness to say, in order that I may practice devout austerities in his honour?" Narada Ji replied,—"Listen Bikasoor! amongst these three deities, Mahadeva is the greatest granter of boons, he neither loves delay, nor is he easily angry. Behold! Shivù Jee, being delighted at the performance on his part of a slight penance, gave a thousand arms to Suhusrajooraun, and destroyed him, being enraged at a slight fault he had committed."

Narada, the sage, having thus spoken went away; and Bikasoor began, when he came home, to perform severe penance and offer up sacrifice in honour of Mahadeva. In the course of seven days, he cut off with a knife, and offered as a burnt offering all the flesh of his body; on the eighth day, when he resolved to cut off his head, Bholanath came, and having laid hold of his hand said,—"I have been highly pleased with thee, ask from me whatever boon thou desirest, and I will now grant it to thee." When Shivù Jee had thus spoken, Bikasoor, with joined hands, replied,—"Be pleased, O lord! to take compassion upon me, and now grant me this boon, that on whose head soever I may place my hand, he may be reduced to ashes instantaneously." On his uttering these words, Mahadeva Jee granted him the boon he had asked; which when he had obtained, he went to put his hand upon Shivù's head; Mahadeva was alarmed, and quitted his seat and fled, and the demon also ran after him, and carried on a close pursuit of Sudashivù. At length Mahadeva went in a state of very great agitation to Vishnu's heaven; seeing, that he was greatly afflicted, Shri Murari, the friend of his worshippers, the lord of paradise, the abode of mercy, took compassion upon him, and assuming the appearance of a brahmin went before Bikasoor and said, "O prince of demons! explain to me why you toil in pursuit of Shivù?" On hearing this question, Bikasoor explained all that had occurred, then Bhagavan said, "O chief of demons! it is very strange that an intelligent person like you should commit error, who believes any thing to be true, which this naked, mad Yogi says, who eats bhang and thornapple; he constantly dwells in cemeteries, rubbing his body with ashes, and having snakes twisted round him; assuming a terrifying appearance, and accompanied by ghosts and goblins, who will believe what he says?" Shri Narayun proceeded to say, "O chief of demons! if you think that what I have said is untrue, place your hand on your own head and see."

O great king! on hearing the lord speak thus, when Bikasoor, who was deprived of sense through the influence of the delusive power, placed his hand upon his own head, he was burnt up, and became a heap of ashes; there were musical rejoicings in the capital of Indra on the death of the demon; and the gods, raising shouts of victory and exultation, began to rain down flowers; the celestial dancers, musicians and choristers celebrated in songs the excellent attributes of Hari, who, having at that time, greatly glorified Mahadeva, allowed him to take leave, and granted Bikasoor salvation.
SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said,—O great king! whosoever shall hear or recite this story, shall doubtlessly obtain beatitude by the favour of Hari and Mahadeva.

89.e: SHRI SHUKADEVA JEE said,—O great king! on one occasion all the sages and saints were sitting on the banks of the Sarasvati engaged in devout austerities and religious sacrifice, when one of them asked the others to do him the favour to say, which was greatest of the three divinities, Brahma, Vishnu or Ganesha. Upon this one said Shivù; another, Vishnu; and a third, Brahma; but they did not all agree in pointing out one of the three as the greatest. Then several great saints and sages said, "We will not be satisfied with any opinions thus expressed; but if any one will go and make trial of these three deities, and pronounce one of them to be virtue, religion and justice personified, we will believe what he says to be true." They all assented to this proposal, and directed Bhrigu, the son of Brahma, to make trial of the three deities and return. When Bhrigu, the sage, had obtained the order, he went first to the world of Brahma, and sat in silence in Brahma's court; he did not make any salutation, nor did he offer praises, nor go round to the right hand by way of adoration. When Brahma, O Raja! saw the impropriety of his son’s conduct, he was very angry, and on the point of cursing him; but abstained through a feeling of natural affection for his son. Then Bhrigu, having seen Brahma powerless through the property of passion, rose up thence, and went to Kuelas, and remained standing at the abode of Shivù and Parbutee. Shivù Jee rose on seeing him, and when he extended his arms to embrace him, Bhrigu sat down; at which Shivù Jee was greatly enraged, and took up his trident to kill him. Shri Parbutee then interceded very earnestly for him; and having fallen at the feet of Mahadeva Jee explained to him, and said, This is your younger brother, be pleased to forgive his fault." It is said, 'If a child commits a fault, a holy man will not think any thing of it.'"

O great king! when Parbutee Jee had cooled the anger of Shivù by her explanations, Bhrigu, having seen Mahadeva Jee, absorbed in the property of darkness, rose up and went away. He then went to Indra's heaven, where Bhagavan was sleeping with Luchmee on a bed of flowers, spread on a bedstead of gold, with curtains and covered with jewels. On going there Bhrigu gave Bhagavan such a kick in the breast that he started up from sleep, when Hari saw the sage, he left Luchmee, and came down from his couch; and fixing his eyes upon the head and feet of Bhrigu Jee began to rub them, and thus address him, "O chief of the sages! be pleased to forgive my fault, I have unintentionally hurt your soft lotus-like feet with my hard breast, be pleased not to think of this offence of mine." When Vishnu (the lord) had thus spoken, Bhrigu Jee was highly delighted, and having glorified Bhagavan took leave and came thence to the banks of the Sarasvati, where all the saints and sages were sitting. On his arrival Bhrigu Jee related every circumstance exactly as it had occurred, in his visits to the three deities:—"Brahma clings to the property of passion; Mahadeva is impregnated with the property of darkness; Vishnu is chief amongst the virtuous; no other god is greater than he." The doubts of the sages disappeared on hearing this; and joy was in the minds of all. All applauded Vishnu and established in their breasts a faith in him not to be shaken.

Having proceeded thus far in the narrative, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said to the Raja Parikshit,—O great king! I will relate an intermediate story, listen with attention: Raja Ugrasena ruled justly and virtuously in the city of Dwarka, and Shri Krishna Chund and Balarama were obedient to his orders; under the government of the Raja all were attentive to their own duty, and carried on business with intelligence, and lived happily and agreeably; a brahmin dwelt there also, who was a very well disposed and virtuous man; it so happened that one of his sons died, and he took his dead son and went to the gate of Raja Ugrasena, and began to say whatever came uppermost: "Your subjects are oppressed by the acts of your government, and my son has also died through your sin."

Having, O great king! made many speeches of this kind, and left the corpse of his son at the Raja’s gate, the brahmin came home; he afterwards had eight sons, and in like manner left all the eight at the Raja’s gate; when the ninth was about to be born, the brahmin went again to the court of Raja Ugrasena, and standing up in the presence of Shri Krishna Chund Jee, calling to mind his grief for the death of his sons, and shedding tears began to say, "There is a curse on the Raja and on his government, and accursed are they who minister to this unjust tyrant; and there is a curse upon me for living in this city had I not dwelt in the country of these sinners my sons would have escaped, through their want of religion and virtue my sons have died, and no one has protected them."

He, O great king! uttered many expressions of this kind, standing up in the court and weeping; but no one made any reply; at length Arjuna, sitting near Shri Krishna Chund, and hearing what was said was perplexed in his mind, and said, "O deity! in whose presence have you thus spoken, and why are you thus afflicted? There is no archer in this court, who can drive away your grief; modern Rajas are selfish, and not men, who prevent the afflictions of others, and confer happiness on their subjects, and protect the cow and brahmin." Arjuna proceeded to say to the brahmin, "O divinity! go now, and remain in your house, free from all care; when your child shall be about to be born come to me, and I will go with you, and will not allow the child to die." On hearing these words, the brahmin was angry and said, "I do not see any powerful man in this court, with exception of Shri Krishna, Balarama, Purdiyomun and Unroodrù, who could rescue my son from the hand of death." Arjuna replied, "Brahmin! thou dost not know me, that my name is Dhununjye, I make a compact with thee, that if I do not rescue thy son from the hand of death, I will bring from whatever quarter I may find them thy deceased sons, and show them to thee; and if I do not obtain them, I will burn myself in fire together with the cow (bow?—JBH) Gandeeb."

When, O great king! Arjuna having made this compact, had thus spoken, the brahmin was satisfied, and went to his home; afterwards when the child was about to be born, the brahmin came to Arjuna, who rose up and went with him, taking his bow and arrows and having gone to the brahmin’s house, so thatched it with arrows, that even air could not have access between the arrows, and he began to walk round the house himself in every direction, with his bow and arrows in his hand.

Having proceeded thus far in the narrative, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said to the Raja Parikshit,—O great king! Arjuna formed many plans for saving the child, but it was not saved. On another day he was weeping at the time of the child’s expected birth; on that day the child did not even breathe, but came forth dead from the womb. Arjuna having heard of the child having come forth dead was ashamed, and went to Shri Krishna Chund, and the brahmin went after him; the brahmin came crying, and began to say, "Arjuna! a curse is upon thee, and thy life for showing thy face in the world, after having spoken falsely; O eunuch! if you could not save my child from death, why did you make an agreement to do so, and to bring and show nee my other deceased sons, if you could not save this one?"

On hearing these words, O great king! Arjuna rose up, and taking his bow and arrows, went thence, to the capital of Jinn to Dhurumraj, who stood up on seeing him, and joining his hands, and eulogizing Arjuna, said,—"O great king! for what reason have you come here?" Arjuna replied, "I have come to take away with me the sons of a certain brahmin." Dhurumraj said "Those children are not here." When Dhurumraj had thus spoken, Arjuna departed thence, and wandered over all places, but did not find the brahmin’s children. A t length, he came to the city of Dwarka in a state of grief and regret; and, having erected a funeral pile, prepared to be burnt upon it with his bow and arrows having then lighted the pile, when Arjuna was about to sit down upon it, Shri Murari, the destroyer of pride, came, and laid hold of his hand, and said laughing, "Arjuna! do not burn thyself, I will fulfil thy compact, and will bring that brahmin’s sons from whatever place they may be in." The lord of the three worlds having thus spoken and ascended his chariot, went to the eastward, taking Arjuna with him; and, having crossed the seven seas, arrived at the mountainous belt, bounding the world. Having on arrival there descended from the chariot, they entered a very dark cave. Then Shri Krishna Chund Jee gave an order to the quoit Sudarshana, who, having created a light, equal to the splendour of hundred million of suns, went in advance of Krishna and dispelled the great darkness from before him. Having left the darkness they proceeded a short distance, and then they went into water; there were great waves into which they entered, shutting their eyes, Krishna and Arjuna swam to the abode of the king of the serpent race, who upholds the world.

Having opened their eyes on going there, they beheld a large, long, broad, lofty, very elegant golden house, covered with jewels; and there, upon the head of the king of the serpent face was an ornamented throne, upon which, in the form of a black cloud, of an elegant shape, with a moon-like body, eyes like the lotus, wearing a diadem and ear-rings, dressed in yellow, with a yellow silken cloth bound on him, having on a garland of flowers reaching to his feet, and a pearl of necklace, the lord himself of a fascinating appearance dwelt; and Brahma, Rudra, Indra and all the gods standing up in his presence, were glorifying him.

O great king! having beheld this handsome figure, Arjuna and Shri Krishna Chund Jee went into the presence of the lord; and, having performed obeisance, and joined their hands, mentioned all the reasons of their journey. On hearing their speech the lord had all the brahmin’s children brought there, and given to them; and Arjuna was delighted at seeing and receiving them. Then the lord said, "You are both portions of my body, behold Hari and Arjuna to whom my heart desires; you went upon the earth to remove its burthens, and have conferred great happiness on holy and virtuous men; you have destroyed all the demons and evil spirits, and adjusted the affairs of gods, men and sages; you both are parts of me; your business has been accomplished." Having thus spoken, Bhagavan allowed Arjuna and Shri Krishna Jee to take leave, who came to the city, bringing the children with them; and the brahmin received his children; there were rejoicings and festivities in every house.
Having recited thus much, SHRI SHUKADEVA Jee said to Raja Parikshit,—O great king! whoever shall hear this story, and reflect upon it, his sons shall be prosperous.
